Recommend a first call, after requesting data. Thesis fit is clean: B2B vertical SaaS, seed, Germany/NL, and the €1.5-2m lead cheque sits inside our 1-4M range. The services angle is the main flag but looks manageable. Cold inbound, no portfolio intro mentioned.

What is in favour: €412k ARR across 19 firms (~€22k ACV). 86% of revenue is subscription, and migration work is priced separately with no recovery-based fees. 7 of 19 firms have expanded seats. No churn yet. Median deployment fell from 8 to 3 weeks. Founders are complementary: Marta ran ops at an insolvency practice for 9 years, Emil built document infrastructure. Her stated plan is to hire engineers rather than more implementers.

What worries me: (1) Retention is unproven. The oldest customer is 14 months in, and Marta says so herself. (2) Market size is the real question. The market is niche, and each new country needs separate court integrations and local rules, so expansion may be slow and costly. (3) Onboarding is hands-on. We need gross margin including migration staff cost, and whether the 3-week deployment still needs ops involvement. (4) Round risk: €650k is verbal only, so our lead cheque matters to closing. (5) Competition from incumbent practice-management vendors is not addressed.

Ask for before the call: subscription vs migration revenue split, monthly cohort and expansion data, gross margin with migration cost loaded, pricing model, pipeline and sales-cycle length, bottom-up TAM for DACH/Benelux plus the two target markets, and the competitor view.

Pass if: ARR includes migration fees, deployment still needs heavy ops time, or the bottom-up market for the next two countries looks too small. Marta's tone is candid and she is not rushing, which is a good sign.

Recommendation: take a call with Noor before Friday. Clear thesis fit and a warm intro from a portfolio founder. Assign someone to review the deck and cohort sheet today.

Why it fits: Stackquay is a Boston-based devtools company (deployment policy enforcement inside existing CI pipelines, with approval audit trail). It is a Series A in B2B software in the US. The ask is €2–3m of an $8m round, inside our €1–4M range.

Traction (as stated by the founder, unverified): $1.9m ARR, up from $710k a year ago (about 2.7x). 34 paying companies, so ACV is roughly $56k.

Intro: Tessa Brandt (Patchharbor founder) has co-built two open-source projects with Noor and has seen Stackquay live at one of her customers. That is a first-hand reference, not just a forward.

Timing: the lead decision is Friday. We would be a non-lead participant alongside a proposed lead, whose name and terms we do not have.

Open questions for the call: who is the lead and what are the terms and valuation; net revenue retention, churn and logo concentration in the cohort sheet; how the product is differentiated from CI-native controls and larger platforms; sales motion and pipeline behind the growth; whether we get a board seat or information rights at this allocation.

Note: I have not seen the attachments. The figures above come from Noor's email only.

Next step: reply to Tessa today to confirm, and ask Noor for call times Wed or Thu.

In scope: B2B fintech infrastructure, EU, seed, and his €1.5m lead slot fits our €1-4M ticket. Cold inbound, no portfolio intro. Facts: Prague, reconciliation and settlement APIs sold to payment providers, no lending and no custody of funds (limits regulatory risk). 9 paying customers, €23k MRR (~€276k ARR, ~€30k ACV each), raising €2.8m. Cofounder previously ran ledger engineering at a payments processor, which is a credible technical fit. Open questions: MRR growth over the last 6-12 months, churn and contract length, customer concentration, sales cycle and pipeline, whether customers are integrated into core flows (stickiness), competition from in-house builds and incumbents, and who else is in the round. Recommendation: take the deck and reply today. Ask for the MRR by customer and monthly trend alongside it. Book a call only if growth and retention hold up. Suggested reply: 'In scope, send the deck plus MRR by customer and monthly trend. We'll respond within a week.'

Recommendation: take the call, but have an associate screen the deck first. It fits the thesis, and the open question is market size, not fit.

Fit: vertical SaaS, B2B, US, seed, with revenue. The ~€2m lead ask is within our 1-4M ticket. Cold inbound with no portfolio intro, so no warm-intro priority.

Numbers: $39k MRR is ~$470k ARR across 42 customers, so ACV is ~$11k. Two churned last quarter, which is ~4-5% quarterly logo churn or ~17% annualized. That is acceptable for SMB but not great for compliance-critical software. He disclosed it upfront, which is a good sign. The $3.5m round on ~$470k ARR is a ~7x ask on a round-size basis, so valuation will depend on growth.

Key risks: (1) TAM: independent elevator contractors are a narrow US niche, so we need a path to $100M ARR through expansion (payments, parts, inspections marketplace) or adjacent trades. (2) Competition from generic field-service tools (ServiceTitan, Jobber, etc.) and OEM in-house systems. (3) Whether churn is concentrated in recent cohorts or in a particular customer size.

Check in the deck before the call: MRR growth over the last 6-12 months, net revenue retention, new-logo sales cycle and CAC, how many of the 42 are multi-year, regulatory stickiness (inspection and compliance records as lock-in), and use of funds.

Pass if growth is under ~2x YoY and there is no credible expansion story. Otherwise take the 20 minutes.

Recommend taking the meeting this week. Fit is clean: Permitloom is B2B vertical SaaS (permit workflow for commercial builders), London-based, at seed with £31k MRR (about £370k ARR). The £3m round (about €3.5m) with a €1.5m lead allocation sits inside our €1-4M ticket range. The intro is warm, from Rafael Costa (Tracebeacon founder), who has known Imani Reed for six years and says he would back her again. Open questions for the call: 1) MRR growth trend and net revenue retention, since we only have a single data point. 2) Customer concentration and sales cycle in construction. 3) Who else is in the round, and whether we are truly leading or just filling an allocation. 4) Defensibility against incumbent construction software and local-authority integration risk. 5) Whether the model can scale beyond the UK. I have not seen the attached deck, so the figures above are unverified and come only from Rafael's email. Next step: reply to Rafael, thank him, and have the team schedule a 30-minute intro call with Imani.

Recommendation: soft pass for now, stay warm. Don't lead.

Fit: Sector (devtools, B2B), geography (Paris) and ticket (€1m lead, at the bottom of our range) all fit.

Problem: Stage. Founders call it seed, but it is pre-seed on the facts: prototype only, four unpaid design partners, no production use, no invoices. The €1.6m raise is large for that traction, so we would be underwriting team and market alone. Our thesis is seed and Series A, and we have no warm intro to justify an exception.

What's unknown: Founder backgrounds, why this debugger beats Datadog, Monte Carlo, or the orchestrator-native tooling (Airflow, Dagster), and whether design partners would pay.

Suggested reply: Honest answer is yes, a bit early for us to lead. Invite them to come back when at least 2 design partners are in production or on paid pilots. Offer to look at the deck if they want feedback, but set expectations that we're unlikely to move before there is paid usage. Ask them to send quarterly updates.

If you want to spend 2 minutes: skim the deck only for founder pedigree and any signal of paid conversion. Strong signs there could justify a call.

Recommendation: take the call this week, with a partner on it. It fits the thesis and comes with a credible warm intro. Leila says first partner meetings are next week, so we should move before then.

Fit: B2B devtools, Series A, Lyon (Europe), subscription only. Her €2-3m lead ask is inside our €1-4M range. No thesis flags.

Intro: Celine Roux (QueryMantle cofounder) referred her and says she already sent a note. Check with Celine before the call. Ask how she knows Leila and how she would rate her.

Numbers as claimed, not yet verified:
- ARR €1.46m, up from €510k a year ago (about 2.9x). 34 customers, so ACV is about €43k.
- NRR 132%, gross margin 88%, one churn (acquisition). 27 of 34 customers added a second database in their first quarter, and median implementation is 4 days. These are the strongest adoption signals.
- Largest customer is 13% of ARR (about €190k). Concentration is acceptable. Three references are offered.
- Team of 8. Both founders are credible for this problem: Boris led database reliability, and Leila has built and sold deployment software. First commercial hire joined in January.

Round: €6m Series A after a €1.4m seed. Lead ask €2-3m plus €1.2m from existing investors, which totals €3.2-4.2m. The remaining €1.8-2.8m is unaccounted for, so ask who fills it. Use is a US sales hire, two more database engines and 24 months of runway.

Key questions:
1. Buying intent vs. developer adoption: who signs, what budget it comes from, and how much is bottom-up vs. sales-led. The only commercial hire is 5 months old, so the sales motion is unproven.
2. Competition and substitutes: database branching and migration tools, in-house CI scripts, and cloud providers adding this natively. Why does Dockscript win and keep winning?
3. Security: customers must trust masked copies of production data. Ask about certifications, how masking works, and any security-driven deal losses.
4. Expansion economics: what drives the 132% NRR (more databases, seats, usage), and how much of it comes from the top 5 accounts?
5. US go-to-market: what a first US hire achieves with 8 people, and the hiring plan beyond that.
6. Round dynamics: who else is meeting them, whether there is a lead already, and what valuation they expect.

Next step: reply with Tuesday or Thursday slots, ask Celine for a quick call, and review the deck and metrics one-pager before the meeting. Ask for the cohort and customer-level ARR data.

Recommendation: reply yes, ask for the deck. In scope, no red flags yet. Fit: B2B fintech infrastructure (reconciliation APIs), Berlin, seed. The €1.5m lead cheque is inside our €1-4M range. Traction: €22k MRR (~€264k ARR) across 9 customers, so ~€2.4k MRR (~€29k ARR) per customer. That is thin for a €3m round and suggests small customers or low pricing. Cold inbound with no portfolio-founder intro, so check whether anyone in our network knows him. Questions for the reply: (1) MRR growth over the last 6 months, (2) net revenue retention and churn, (3) customer mix: processors vs. merchants/PSP resellers, and the largest customer's share of MRR, (4) pricing model and whether usage scales with customer volume, (5) pipeline and sales cycle, (6) valuation expectations and who else is in the round, (7) competition and why customers pick Splitrail over in-house builds or Modern Treasury-type tools. Proposed reply: 'Thanks Niko, please send the deck. Please also include MRR by month, customer list with ACV, retention, and round terms.'

Recommendation: take the call. It fits the thesis on every screen: B2B vertical SaaS, Copenhagen, seed, a €3.5m round with a €1-2m lead ask inside our €1-4M ticket. It is a cold inbound, not a portfolio intro.

What's good: €640k ARR across 21 groups is about €30k ACV. Gross margin is 91%. Six referral conversions suggest early pull. Founder fit is strong (cofounder ran quality systems at a diagnostics group, CEO built compliance software). Use of funds is integrations plus two sales hires, which is a go-to-market bet, not R&D.

What to test on the call: (1) Market size: how many independent lab groups exist in Europe and the US, and how much of that is reachable at ~€30k ACV? Niche vertical risk is the main concern. (2) Retention: ask for net and gross revenue retention by cohort, and check the deck. (3) Growth: ARR a year ago, and new ARR per quarter. (4) Sales motion: does outbound work without Beatrice personally? Ask about cycle length, win rate and the sales hire plan. (5) Referrals: six conversions is small, so ask what drives them and whether they are repeatable. (6) Competition: LIMS vendors adding accreditation modules, and generic QMS tools such as Qualio and MasterControl. Why does Auditgrove win? (7) Integrations: which ones, and are they a moat or a cost of entry? (8) Round: who else is in, and is there a lead or a close date?

Main risks: a small customer count, founder-led sales so far, and a niche TAM that may cap the outcome unless it expands into adjacent regulated testing.

Next step: reply this week to book the 25 minutes, ask for the workflow demo, and request the cohort data and pipeline detail beforehand.

Recommend: take a 20-30 min intro call after a quick deck skim. Cold inbound, no mutual connection, but it fits the thesis. Fit: B2B devtools for regulated engineering teams (release approvals, policy checks, evidence capture in CI), seed stage, Boston (US). Revenue: $41k MRR (~$490k ARR) from 16 customers, so ~$2.6k MRR (~$31k ACV) per customer. Round: $4m seed with $1.5-2m open for a new investor, which sits inside our 1-4M EUR ticket. Unknowns (deck not reviewed): MRR growth rate and history, logo/net retention, sales cycle and who buys (eng, security or compliance), who is leading and at what valuation, and how it differs from incumbents (CI-native approval/environment features, change-management tools like ServiceNow, and Harness-type platforms). Risks: crowded adjacent category, and ACV may need to rise for venture-scale outcomes. Before the call: ask for the deck's growth and retention numbers, and check whether any portfolio founder knows her to get a warm reference. Suggested reply: yes to a call next week, ask for monthly MRR by customer and the lead/term status.

Recommendation: take a 20-30 min call today. It fits the mandate, but treat the deadline as his pressure, not ours. Fit: B2B fintech infrastructure, US, Series A. A $2m allocation (about 1.85M EUR) is at the low end of our 1-4M EUR range. Signals: $2.3m ARR across 29 customers is about $80k per customer. There is a signed lead term sheet, but the lead is unnamed. Cold inbound with no warm intro, so ask our portfolio founders whether anyone knows Caleb or Vaultspan. I have not seen the deck. Questions to settle on the call: 1) Who is the lead, and what are the valuation and terms? 2) ARR growth, net revenue retention and logo churn. 3) Revenue model: SaaS fees vs. take rate on funds held, and gross margin. 4) Concentration: top customers' share of ARR, and how many banking partners there are and how easily they can be swapped. 5) Regulatory position: who holds the licenses, and whether Vaultspan carries any money-transmission or compliance exposure. 6) Is the allocation firm, and can we get a data room and references today? Decision rule: if the lead is credible, retention is strong and bank dependence is manageable, do fast diligence and decide by tomorrow. If answers are vague or we can't verify the lead, pass without regret.

Inbound from Ruth Ellison (Coverstitch, Manchester), cold, no portfolio intro. Recommendation: take a short call or reply only on a software-only basis. As pitched, it is outside thesis.

Facts: Vertical SaaS for commercial insurance brokers (specialist contractor cover quoting and renewals). 14 brokers, £19k MRR (about £228k ARR). Separately, £1.8m annualised written premium via an affiliated underwriter that sets prices and retains some risk. Team of 7, with 5 on product. Raising £3m seed with a £1-1.5m lead (about €1.2-1.75m, within our ticket range). Geography and stage fit.

Issue: The investment would go into a holdco that owns both the software and the risk-bearing underwriting business. Our mandate is B2B software only. Carrier risk, regulatory capital and loss volatility are not software economics. Ruth is candid that premium is not software revenue, which is a good sign.

Key questions before spending time:
1. Is the software company being separated before closing? We should only invest in the software entity, or in a holdco with the underwriter ring-fenced or excluded.
2. Does the software work without the affiliate? Do brokers pay for software that is independently useful, or is it a distribution front end for the affiliate's capacity and pricing?
3. Who owns the pricing and underwriting IP and data, and what related-party agreements exist between the two businesses?
4. What is the regulatory status (FCA authorisations, delegated authority), and how much capital is at risk on the retained share?
5. Of the £19k MRR, how much comes from brokers who use only the software versus those who also place business with the affiliate?

Proposed reply: Thank her for the clarity. Say we invest only in software businesses and can't consider the combined holdco. Ask her to send the structure diagram and deck, and say we would look further only if the software entity is separated. Keep it brief and don't commit time yet.

Recommendation: soft pass for now, keep warm. Reply briefly and ask for an update when the two procurement processes close.

What it is: Benchsignal sells regression testing for speech models (replay audio, compare failure rates by accent and environment, block bad releases). Three cofounders in Rotterdam. Cold inbound, no portfolio intro. Raising €1.8m with a hoped-for €1.2m lead.

Thesis fit: Devtools, B2B software, Europe, no hardware or labeling. The €1.2m lead is within our €1-4M ticket. The product is in scope. Stage is the issue.

Traction: Live 11 weeks. 14 teams, 6 running weekly tests, 3 piloting. €9.6k invoiced in total, no annual contracts, so no ARR. Test minutes went from 31k to 82k month on month, but that includes free accounts. Only one pilot has it in its release pipeline. Another still reviews the CSV by hand.

Why not now: This is pre-seed by our standards. There is no paid conversion yet and no proof that usage turns into contracts. The round is undefined: no instrument, no valuation, no committed investor, and their own angels disagree on whether it is seed or pre-seed. A €1.2m lead cheque into that is early for us.

Positives: Honest about numbers, and the founders do not inflate ARR. Credible founder-market fit (test infrastructure plus acoustics research). One customer has embedded it in CI, which is the behavior we want to see. 20 months of runway on the plan.

Risks to check later: Consented voice data raises GDPR and biometric-data exposure, and we would need to see how consent is handled. There is no sales hire and no US entity, and the plan leans on one solutions engineer. The customer base is narrow (teams shipping speech models). Need to see whether usage reflects budget or free trials.

Suggested reply: Recurring revenue is not a hard prerequisite, but we need signed paid conversion before leading. Suggest they come back once one or both procurement processes close as annual contracts, ideally with a cohort split of paid vs free usage. Offer to look at the cohort table now if they want a quick read, but do not commit time to a call.

Recommendation: ask for the deck. It's a clean thesis fit, but it's a cold inbound with no portfolio intro, so check whether any of our founders know Theo. Fit: B2B devtools (CI cost control), Boston, seed, $410k ARR with 28 paying customers. The ask of a €1-2m lead on a $3.2m round sits inside our 1-4M EUR ticket range. Implied ACV is about $14.6k, so it's likely SMB or mid-market engineering teams. Questions for the first look: (1) ARR growth over the last 6-12 months, plus net revenue retention and logo churn. (2) Sales motion (self-serve or product-led versus sales-led) and payback. (3) Platform risk: GitHub, GitLab and CircleCI could build native cost controls, so what is the moat? (4) Savings delivered to customers versus price, to show ROI. (5) Valuation, who else is in the round, and how much is committed. Next step: reply asking for the deck and a metrics snapshot, and take a 30-minute call if retention and growth hold up.

Recommend taking the 25-minute call. Cold inbound, no portfolio intro. It fits the thesis: B2B vertical SaaS, Hamburg, Series A, and a €2-3m lead sits inside our €1-4m range. It is subscription software, not fintech or marketplace, and there is no success fee or receivables exposure.

Claimed numbers (unverified): €1.46m ARR, up from €790k (+85% YoY). 46 customers, median €24k, largest €118k (~8% of ARR). GRR 94%, NRR 116%, gross margin 83%. Implementation cut from 51 to 24 days. 13 staff, 9 in product and engineering. Raising €6m, with €1.5m existing-investor follow-on conditional on a lead. 11 months of runway. Break-even at ~€4m ARR.

Positives: retention and margin are solid for this stage. Pricing is a fixed subscription, so revenue does not depend on dispute outcomes. Founders have domain depth (8 years in forwarding software; invoice operations). The wedge is clear: independent forwarders with 20-150 ops staff. They are also disciplined about scope, declining to build a TMS.

Concerns: (1) ARR is at the low end for an A, and 85% growth is good but not exceptional. (2) Sales is founder-led (Saskia runs most late-stage demos), so repeatability is unproven. (3) The plan depends on integrations with two major TMS vendors, which creates platform risk and a risk that TMS vendors bundle the feature. (4) UK/US expansion with a small commercial team is a stretch. (5) The €6m round needs ~€2-3m beyond our cheque and the existing €1.5m, so we would need to bring in or find co-investors. (6) Losses to full-TMS replacements may point to a ceiling on the segment.

Ask on the call or in the data: cohort churn and logo vs revenue retention; ARR by segment and sales-cycle length; how many customers came from founder-led sales vs inbound; pipeline and win rate; the TMS partner dependency and whether any have commitments; how much of the 24-day implementation is customer-side delay; evidence of customer ROI (disputes found vs. cost); and ARR definition (contracted, excluding pilots).

Next step: reply to schedule the call, and have an associate review the deck and metrics sheet beforehand. Ask for a customer reference list. Check whether anyone in our portfolio works with freight forwarders and could give a back-channel view.

Recommendation: ask for the deck and take a 30-minute intro call. It fits the thesis and the cheque size.

Fit: Tallysocket sells reconciliation APIs to B2B payment platforms, which is fintech infrastructure. It is based in Dublin (Europe) and is raising a €3m seed. Nessa wants a €1.5m lead, which is inside our €1-4M ticket range. It has revenue (not pre-revenue), and she says it is not consumer, lending or wallet.

Traction: 11 customers and €36k MRR (about €430k ARR), or roughly €3.3k MRR (about €39k ACV) per customer. She says none of the MRR is transaction revenue, so it appears to be SaaS or API subscription revenue. That is early but credible for a seed.

Caveats:
- It is a cold inbound with no portfolio intro. She found us while building an investor list, so it is not a targeted approach.
- She gave no growth rate, retention, customer concentration, sales cycle or team background.
- Competition is unclear. Candidates include Modern Treasury, in-house builds at payment platforms, and other reconciliation vendors.

Next step: reply yes to the deck. Ask for MRR by month for the last 12 months, net revenue retention, top-3 customer share, pipeline, and the current lead or investor status. Check our portfolio founders for a reference on her before the call.

Lintcove (Prague): thesis fit, worth a 20-min call, but diligence is compressed. Recommend: take the call, don't commit to the Thursday 17:00 CET deadline until the data checks out.

Fit: B2B devtools/security-adjacent, Series A, Europe. €2m allocation is inside our €1-4M range. Not consumer, hardware or climate.

Claims (unverified): €2.2m ARR, 71 customers (~€31k average ACV), €7m round, lead already signed, €2m left. Cold inbound, no portfolio intro. I haven't seen the attachments (deck, cohorts, draft terms), so the figures above are Marek's own.

Before or on the call, get:
1) Lead investor name and signed term sheet status. Confirm the lead is real and ask who else is in the remaining allocation.
2) Valuation, pro-rata, and any side terms in the draft terms.
3) YoY ARR growth, net and gross retention, and logo churn by cohort. Dependency-policy tools face open-source competition (Dependabot, Renovate, Snyk), so ask about pricing power and win rates.
4) Customer concentration and the share of ARR on annual contracts vs pilots.
5) Burn, runway and use of funds.

Risks: the deadline pressure is a mild flag, since a €2m ticket is a big commitment on two days' diligence. A €2m allocation in a €7m round probably means no board seat, so our influence would be limited. Also ask a portfolio founder in devtools/security for a quick reference or customer intro.

Next step: reply today to book the call tomorrow morning. Ask Marek to send the lead's name and the data room link beforehand. Pass if the lead can't be confirmed or retention is weak.

Recommendation: reply yes, ask for the deck, and take a 30-min call if the metrics hold up. Fit: B2B fintech infrastructure, Berlin, seed, €3m round with a €1-2m lead cheque, all inside our thesis and ticket range. Traction: €290k ARR across 11 paying payment platforms, about €26k average ACV. That is real revenue, but early. Caveats: this is a cold inbound with no portfolio-founder intro, and the email gives no growth rate, retention, or customer concentration. Check first in the deck: 1) ARR growth over the last 12 months and the monthly trend. 2) Net revenue retention and logo churn. 3) Concentration, i.e. whether the top 2-3 customers are more than 50% of ARR. 4) Pricing model (usage vs. platform fee) and whether ACV is expanding. 5) Sales cycle and how the 11 customers were won (founder-led vs. repeatable). 6) Competition: Modern Treasury-type players, incumbents, and in-house builds. 7) Round status: who else is in, whether a lead is already committed, and the timeline. Next step: ask a portfolio founder in payments for a back-channel reference on Settleweft while the deck comes in.

Recommend taking the meeting. Yardfolio is London-based vertical SaaS for commercial landscaping contractors (quoting, crew scheduling, renewals), which fits the thesis. Jonah Vale (Mergehollow, portfolio) is vouching from four years of working with Ellis. The €2-3m allocation sits inside our €1-4m ticket. Stated metrics: £1.4m ARR, 83 customers (about £17k ACV), 116% NRR, 74% gross margin, raising £6m. I have not seen the deck or cohort table; these figures come from Ellis's email. Concerns to test: (1) ARR is on the small side for a £6m A, so growth rate and burn matter most. (2) 74% gross margin is low for SaaS, so ask whether onboarding, support or payments is dragging it. (3) Competition from Jobber, LMN and Aspire, and how big the UK/Europe market is without a US move. (4) Logo churn versus NRR, since expansion can hide churn in a small base. (5) Seasonality, CAC payback and sales cycle. (6) Lead status: we'd be a €2-3m participant, so who is leading and at what valuation? Next step: reply to Jonah with thanks, ask Ellis for a call, and have someone review the cohort table before it.

Recommendation: take the call. In scope on every axis: B2B devtools, Amsterdam, seed, and a €1.5–2.5m lead sits inside our €1–4M ticket range. Cold inbound with no portfolio intro, so no warm-intro priority. Traction: €420k ARR 9 months after launch, 31 paying customers, 89% gross margin, 6 expansions from one team to company-wide. Q-o-Q new bookings were €118k ARR, mostly inbound from their open-source config diff library, so acquisition is cheap so far. Team of 5, full-time, with relevant backgrounds (Vera: release infra at a payments processor; Bram: DevEx at a database company). Round is €3.5m with 14 months of runway, so no urgency pressure. Risks: (1) 18% of ARR is one account, about €76k. (2) 3 small-customer churns from layoffs; need logo and net revenue retention by cohort. (3) Sales repeatability is untested: growth is OSS-led and the first commercial hire is not yet made. (4) Larger deals took about a month because of security reviews, which will limit enterprise velocity. (5) Crowded category: feature-flag vendors, observability platforms and incident tools could add change tracking. The wedge needs to be sharp. (6) No valuation stated. Questions for the call: NRR and gross retention by cohort; OSS-to-paid conversion and what share of the 31 customers came from OSS; ACV distribution and the top-5 customer share; why customers buy this instead of an observability or flag vendor add-on; the roadmap to SOC 2 and other security requirements; use of proceeds against a 12–18 month plan; who else is in the round and how much of the lead they want. Ask them to send the deck cohort data ahead of time. Prefer the live demo over slides.

Recommend: take the 20 min this week. Fit is clean. Railcairn (Paris) builds treasury-routing APIs for B2B platforms, which is fintech infrastructure. It has revenue (€360k ARR) and is raising a €3m seed with a €1-2m lead slot, inside our €1-4M ticket. The intro is warm: Mira Dalen (Testgrove, portfolio) introduced it and is cc'd. Before the call: (1) Ask Mira for a 2-line view on Selma and the product, and confirm she made the intro. (2) Check the ARR trajectory: growth over the last 6-12 months, net revenue retention, and customer concentration. (3) Regulatory model: does Railcairn hold its own licenses or rely on bank/EMI partners, and how dependent is it on them? (4) Who else is in the round, and does the lead slot assume we lead or co-lead? Risks: €360k ARR is early, and the pitch is silent on traction quality and on regulatory exposure. Neither rules out a call. Suggested reply: accept, offer two slots, and cc Mira.

Recommendation: take a short screening call, but do not commit to Friday. The fit is real, the process risk is that we would be a passive follower in someone else's round.

What it is: Rosterfen, Chicago. Operating software (scheduling, dispatch, compliance reports, renewals) for commercial fire-inspection firms. Cold inbound, no intro. Raising $8m Series A, US fund has a signed lead term sheet, and we are offered a ~€2m allocation. The deadline is Friday.

Thesis fit: Yes. B2B vertical SaaS, Series A, US, and €2m is inside our 1-4M range. It does not breach any exclusion.

Numbers (all self-reported, unverified):
- $2.8m ARR, up from $1.6m (+75% YoY). Implementation fees ($140k) are excluded, which is clean.
- 126 customers, so ACV is about $22k.
- 84% gross margin, 119% NRR, largest customer 7% of revenue.
- 16 months of runway, so the deadline is about allocation, not survival.
- 17 people. The CEO has 7 years running an inspection operator, and the cofounder ran delivery at a facilities platform. Good founder-market fit.

Concerns:

Recommendation: take the call. In-thesis and worth 30 minutes, but not a clear yes. It's a cold inbound, not a portfolio intro.

Fit: Vertical SaaS for independent flour mills. Subscription only, no hardware. France, Belgium and US. The €2.5-3.5m lead ask sits inside our 1-4M ticket range.

Numbers (company-reported, unverified): ARR €1.46m, +91% YoY. Gross margin 79%. NRR 116%. 43 paying sites, so about €34k ACV. Top customer is 12% of ARR (~€175k). US is 18% of revenue (~€260k). Two churns in 12 months (plant closure, reverted to a parent's in-house system). Team of 12. Raising €6m, with seed investors in for €1m. Runway is about 14 months, so there's no deadline pressure.

Positives: Clear wedge (traceability, driven by audit deadlines) with an expansion path into inventory and planning. Churn looks benign. Services revenue (€112k) is kept out of ARR. Founders have real domain depth: Sabine ran delivery for food processors, Benicio led engineering at an industrial workflow software company, and the head of customer success ran QA at a milling group. The deck is candid about weaknesses.

Concerns:
1. Market ceiling. Independent mills are a narrow base. At ~€34k ACV, a venture-scale outcome needs either a large US footprint or expansion into other food processors. She says she doesn't want to pad the TAM, which is credible but makes the size question central.
2. Onboarding. Median go-live is 7 weeks, and two projects ran past 12. Historic lot data is the bottleneck, and the fix is unproven. This drags on CAC payback, margin and US scalability.
3. Scale. €1.46m ARR is light for an A. The case rests on growth quality and the US motion, which is still unproven.
4. US sales motion is the stated use of funds, but US is only 18% of revenue today. We need to see how those sites were won.
5. Gross margin of 79% is below the SaaS norm. Likely implementation and contractor costs; check.
6. Concentration. The top customer is 12% of ARR, which is large relative to ~€34k average ACV, so it's probably a multi-site group.

Ask on the call: monthly burn and net new ARR; CAC and payback by region; logo churn and expansion by cohort; cohort go-live times and the impact of the import tools; how the US sites were won and the pipeline; the top-customer contract; the TAM build (mills by country, adjacent segments, pricing); valuation expectations; and who else is looking at the round.

Next step: Reply to Sabine with times this or next week. Have the team review the revenue bridge before the call. Pass if the TAM logic doesn't clear roughly €30m+ ARR potential or if the onboarding fix isn't credible.

Before or on the call:

2. Check the deck's revenue mix to confirm the no-brokerage claim. Any transaction or commission revenue would change the profile.
3. Get growth rate (YoY and net new ARR), NRR/GRR, logo churn and customer concentration.
